title: ARE MODERN-DAY PROPHETS BIBLICAL?
paragraphs:
ARE MODERN-DAY PROPHETS BIBLICAL?
Before You Say “God Told Me,” Read This—Because Not Every Voice That Sounds Spiritual Came From God
There are few sentences more powerful in Christian circles than these:
“God told me.”
Four words.
And suddenly the conversation changes.
Because how do you argue with God?
Someone says, “God told me you should marry me.”
“God told me to start this ministry.”
“God told me you need to give.”
“God showed me what is going to happen.”
“The Lord told me what you need to do.”
And sometimes the person speaking may sincerely believe it.
Sometimes they may even be right about something.
But sincerity is not Scripture.
Accuracy alone is not proof of divine authority.
Charisma is not confirmation.
A large following is not confirmation.
A title is not confirmation.
And saying “Thus says the Lord” does not automatically mean the Lord said anything.
That is precisely why this question matters.
Are modern-day prophets biblical?

The answer requires more care than a quick “yes” or “no,” because faithful Christians who affirm the full authority of Scripture have reached different conclusions about whether the New Testament gift of prophecy continues today.
But there is something Christians on every side of that debate desperately need to remember:
God never commands His people to surrender discernment.
He commands us to use it.
Paul wrote:
“Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:20–21
The Greek is striking.
“Prophecies” is προφητείας (prophēteias).
And “test” comes from δοκιμάζω (dokimazō)—to examine, test, prove, or determine genuineness.
In other words, biblical faith is not gullibility dressed in Christian vocabulary.
The church is not commanded to believe every supernatural claim.
We are commanded to test.
And that becomes uncomfortable when the person claiming divine revelation is someone we admire.
Someone with a microphone.
Someone with millions of views.
Someone who seems unusually spiritual.
Someone whose conference fills stadiums.
Someone whose predictions occasionally appear astonishing.
Or perhaps someone sitting across from you at church saying quietly:
“God gave me a word for you.”
The moment somebody claims to speak for God, the stakes become enormous.
Because throughout Scripture, God takes His words seriously.
Very seriously.
Jeremiah lived among people who claimed divine revelation while speaking from their own imagination.
God said:
“I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, ‘I have dreamed, I have dreamed!’”
—Jeremiah 23:25
Then comes a chilling description:
“Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully.”
—Jeremiah 23:28
That distinction still matters.
There is an enormous difference between:
“I think God may be leading me…”
and:
“God said.”
One leaves room for human fallibility.
The other invokes divine authority.
And we should tremble before casually putting words into the mouth of the Almighty.
The Old Testament Hebrew word commonly translated “prophet” is נָבִיא (nāḇîʾ).
Biblical prophets were not simply motivational speakers with spiritual intuition.
They were commissioned messengers.
Again and again Scripture introduces prophetic revelation with words equivalent to:
“Thus says the LORD.”
כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה
Ko amar YHWH.
“Thus says the LORD.”
That is not branding.
That is authority.
And Scripture gives severe warnings about falsely claiming that authority.
Deuteronomy 18 warns Israel about the prophet who presumptuously speaks a word God has not commanded.
Jeremiah condemns prophets who speak “visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.”
Ezekiel speaks against those who “follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing.”
That should make every Christian slow down before saying:
“God told me.”
But now we come to the New Testament.
Because something extraordinary happens.
At Pentecost, Peter explains the outpouring of the Holy Spirit by quoting the prophet Joel:
“And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh…”
Then:
“your sons and your daughters shall prophesy…”
—Acts 2:17
Later, Acts describes prophets in the early church.
Agabus is specifically named.
Acts 13 mentions “prophets and teachers” at Antioch.
Acts 21 tells us that Philip the evangelist had four unmarried daughters “who prophesied.”
Paul discusses prophecy extensively in 1 Corinthians 12–14.
So Christians cannot honestly pretend prophecy disappears the moment we turn the page from Malachi to Matthew.
It is clearly present in the New Testament church.

But neither may we simply assume that every person today calling himself or herself “Prophet” possesses the same authority as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Peter, Paul, or the foundational witnesses through whom God gave Scripture.
That is where discernment becomes essential.
Paul writes that the church was:
—Ephesians 2:20
Notice the imagery.
Foundation.
A foundation is laid.
Jesus Christ remains the cornerstone.
The apostles occupied a unique, foundational role in redemptive history.
And whatever position Christians take concerning contemporary prophecy, nobody today gets to write another Gospel of Matthew.
Nobody gets to add another chapter to Romans.
Nobody gets to stand beside Scripture and announce:
“My revelation carries equal authority.”
The canon is not waiting for your favorite preacher's sequel.
Scripture remains the measuring line.
This is why Isaiah's ancient words remain so relevant:
“To the teaching and to the testimony!”
—Isaiah 8:20
And why Paul could tell Timothy that the sacred writings are able to make him “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus,” before declaring:
“All Scripture is breathed out by God…”
—2 Timothy 3:16
The Greek word translated “breathed out by God” is θεόπνευστος (theopneustos).
God-breathed.
That is an extraordinary category.
Your impressions are not theopneustos.
My feelings are not theopneustos.
A preacher's dream is not automatically theopneustos.
A viral prophecy is not theopneustos.
Scripture is.
And this distinction could save someone from enormous spiritual damage.
Because perhaps you have been wounded by someone who weaponized the phrase:
“God told me.”
Maybe somebody manipulated you with prophecy.
Maybe someone predicted something that never happened, then quietly changed the explanation afterward.
Maybe someone used spiritual authority to control your relationship.
Your money.
Your decisions.
Your conscience.
Maybe you were afraid to question them because you thought questioning them meant questioning God.
Listen carefully.
Testing a claimed revelation is not rebellion against God.
God Himself tells you to test.
The apostle John writes:
—1 John 4:1
Why?
“For many false prophets have gone out into the world.”
John did not say:
Believe everything supernatural.
He said:
Test it.
And his immediate test is profoundly Christ-centered.
What does this message say about Jesus Christ?
Because biblical prophecy never exists to make the prophet the star.
The Spirit glorifies Christ.
Jesus said concerning the Holy Spirit:
“He will glorify me.”
—John 16:14
That single truth exposes much of what passes for spirituality.
If someone's “prophetic ministry” constantly makes you obsessed with the prophet instead of Christ…
Be careful.
If you need their next livestream more desperately than you need Scripture…
Be careful.
If questioning their words is treated as questioning God…
Be careful.
If every revelation somehow ends with money flowing toward them…
Be careful.
If Jesus becomes background scenery while the personality on the stage becomes indispensable…
Something has gone terribly wrong.
The Holy Spirit does not come to build celebrity kingdoms.
He glorifies Jesus.
And here we must deal fairly with an important disagreement among Bible-believing Christians.

Some Christians are cessationists. Broadly speaking, they believe certain revelatory or sign gifts associated with the apostolic era no longer function in the church in the same way after the foundational apostolic period.

Other Christians are continuationists. They believe gifts such as prophecy continue, while insisting that contemporary prophetic impressions must be tested and cannot rival, correct, supplement, or override Scripture.
There are thoughtful, Christ-loving Christians on both sides.
So this article will not pretend a centuries-old theological discussion can be solved with a slogan.
But whichever position you hold, Scripture gives boundaries that cannot safely be ignored.
No modern revelation outranks Scripture.
No prophecy may contradict the Gospel.
No prophet becomes spiritually untouchable.
No supernatural manifestation proves by itself that God authorized the messenger.
No Christian should surrender conscience and biblical discernment to someone merely because that person claims divine revelation.
And Jesus Himself gave us an even more frightening warning.
“False christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders…”
—Matthew 24:24
Think about that.
Jesus did not say deception would always look ridiculous.
Sometimes deception looks supernatural.
That means “something incredible happened” is not enough.
Signs are not the ultimate test.
Jesus is.
Truth is.
Scripture is.
The Gospel is.
Character matters too.
Jesus said:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
—Matthew 7:16
Not merely by their predictions.
Not by their followers.
Not by their stage presence.
Fruit.
And what does the Spirit produce?
“Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.”
—Galatians 5:22–23
So perhaps the question should not merely be:
“Can this prophet tell me something about my future?”
Perhaps we should also ask:
Does this ministry make much of Christ?
Does it honor Scripture?
Does it produce repentance?
Does it display humility?
Is there accountability?
Can the leader be questioned?
Are failed claims acknowledged honestly?
Is money handled transparently?
Does the teaching lead people toward Jesus—or dependence upon the prophet?
Because there is something more important than knowing what will happen next Tuesday.
Knowing Christ.
We sometimes become so desperate for a word about tomorrow that we neglect the Word God has already given us today.
We want God to tell us who we will marry.
Meanwhile Scripture tells us how to love.
We want God to reveal our next career move.
Meanwhile Scripture tells us to work faithfully and honestly.
We want a prophecy about financial breakthrough.
Meanwhile Jesus warns us about greed.
We want someone to reveal our destiny.
Meanwhile Jesus says:
“Follow me.”
Maybe the most neglected revelation in some Christian lives is the Bible sitting unopened beside the bed.
And perhaps that hurts because we would rather receive a mysterious secret than obey a clear command.
“Forgive.”
We want another word.
“Repent.”
Another prophecy.
“Love your enemies.”
Something deeper, Lord.
“Take up your cross and follow me.”
And suddenly the problem is not that God has been silent.
The problem is that what He has already said costs us something.
That is where this conversation stops being about famous prophets on the internet.
Now it becomes about us.
Because there is another danger hiding underneath our obsession with prophetic voices.
Sometimes we want certainty more than we want God.
We are terrified of making the wrong decision.
Terrified of tomorrow.
Terrified of losing someone.
Terrified of suffering.
So when someone appears and says, “God showed me your future,” something inside us desperately wants to believe.
Not necessarily because we love truth.
Because we hate uncertainty.
And that fear can make us vulnerable.
But Christianity was never an invitation to control tomorrow.
It was an invitation to trust Jesus with tomorrow.
Faith does not mean knowing everything that is coming.
Faith means knowing the One who will still be there when it comes.
Maybe nobody has a prophetic word about your next five years.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you do not know whether the door will open.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe your prayer has not been answered the way you hoped.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe the diagnosis frightened you.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe someone you trusted failed you.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe a preacher disappointed you.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe somebody once spoke “God's will” over your life and those words became chains around your soul.
Jesus is still Lord.
And Jesus did not die so that another human being could become the mediator you cannot live without.
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
—1 Timothy 2:5
One mediator.
Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because Scripture is filled with people whose lives looked finished.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Scandal.
Then the risen Christ restored him.
Grace.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Scandal.
Then Jesus confronted him, saved him, and transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
Grace.
The Samaritan woman's history was complicated and exposed.
Scandal.
Then she encountered Jesus and ran toward the very people she might once have avoided.
Grace.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Scandal.
Then he turned toward the crucified King and heard words of paradise.
Grace.
That is the Gospel.
Not humanity climbing high enough to become impressive to God.
God coming down in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The greatest message Christianity has for you is not:
“A prophet knows your future.”
It is:
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
That is the announcement that shattered history.
That is the message demons hate.
That is the hope death cannot swallow.
That is the Word your shame cannot cancel.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ returning.
And if you have spent years chasing spiritual experiences while quietly running from Jesus, come home.
If your Bible has gathered dust while prophetic videos filled your history, come home.
If you have made an idol out of a minister, come home.
If someone manipulated you in God's name and you became afraid of Christianity itself, look beyond the person who wounded you and look again at Christ.
If you have claimed “God told me” when, deep inside, you knew it was your own desire speaking…
Repent.
There is grace even here.
Because repentance is not God's invitation to humiliation without hope.
It is His call out of darkness.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance—the language of a changed mind and turning that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Jesus does not expose sin merely to crush sinners.
He exposes darkness so we can stop hiding in it.
And maybe this article has exposed something.
Maybe you have followed voices more closely than you have followed Jesus.
Maybe you trusted personalities because reading Scripture for yourself felt harder.
Maybe someone told you what you desperately wanted to hear.
Maybe you have secretly been afraid that without a “prophetic word,” God will forget you.
He has not forgotten you.
You do not need spiritual theatrics to convince Jesus that you exist.
He knows your name.
He knows the sin you hide.
He knows the wound nobody sees.
He knows why you keep smiling when your soul feels exhausted.
He knows the questions you are afraid to say aloud.
And He still calls sinners to Himself.
Not to a personality.
Not to a platform.
Not to a prophetic celebrity.
To Himself.
Jesus said:
“Come to me…”
—Matthew 11:28
That invitation still stands.
Come to Christ.
Bring your questions.
Bring your disappointment.
Bring your skepticism.
Bring your wounds from church.
Bring your hidden sin.
Bring the parts of your story you wish could be deleted.
Bring the scandal.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories that looked finished.
Not by pretending sin never mattered.
By paying for sin with His own blood.
At the cross, grace was not cheap.
It cost Christ everything.
And the resurrection announces that sin, Satan, shame, and death do not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So are modern-day prophets biblical?

Scripture unquestionably records prophecy as a genuine work of God and a gift present in the New Testament church. Faithful Christians disagree about whether and in what sense that gift continues today.
But Scripture leaves us no permission to be undiscerning.
Test every claim.
Hold tightly to Scripture.
Reject anything contradicting God's revealed Word and the apostolic Gospel.
Look at fruit.
Beware spiritual manipulation.
Never elevate a human messenger above Jesus.
And never let someone's claim of private revelation steal the authority belonging to God's written Word.
Perhaps the safest sentence some Christians could learn again is not:
“God told me.”
But:
“Scripture says.”
Then open the Bible.
Read it in context.
Handle it faithfully.
And point people toward Christ.
If this exposed something you have been afraid to admit, do not hide behind religious language.
And if you have ever been manipulated by someone claiming to speak for God, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your wound. But you can simply say, “Jesus, lead me into truth.”
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not alone.
Not because every sentence here deserves unquestioned acceptance—it does not.
Send it privately to the person who has quietly wondered, “Am I allowed to question this?”
Yes.
Open the Bible together.
Test everything.
Keep Christ at the center.
We want this community to be a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment—not personality worship.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace is not merchandise.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
—Ephesians 2:8
Your greatest need is not access to another prophet.
Your greatest need is Christ.
So open your Bible.
Test the voices.
Refuse manipulation.
Repent when you are wrong.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Hold fast to what is good.
And follow Jesus even when nobody can tell you exactly what tomorrow holds.
Because you do not need to know every detail of tomorrow when you belong to the One who already stands there.
And when every other voice eventually falls silent, there is still one voice your soul cannot afford to miss:
The voice of the Shepherd calling you home.
